title: A Birefringence-Blind Consistency Test of the Planck Cosmic Birefringence Hint
speaker: Anto I. Lonappan (UCSD)
abstract:
Abstract:
Several analyses of Planck, ACT, and WMAP data report a small uniform rotation of CMB polarization, β ≈ 0.3–0.4°. If real, this would be evidence of parity-violating physics such as axion-like fields coupled to photons. At this level, however, the signal is exactly degenerate with an overall miscalibration of the detectors' polarization angles. The leading method, the Minami–Komatsu (MK) likelihood, breaks this degeneracy by using Galactic dust as a calibrator. That makes its detector angles, and therefore β, dependent on how the dust EB correlation is modeled.

In this talk, I will present a complementary test that never uses that foreground model. For any pair of maps, the cosmic rotation cancels exactly, leaving only the relative instrumental angle. We measure these relative angles from antisymmetric and symmetric cross-spectra. We then combine all pairs into a gauge-fixed calibration network, with maps as nodes and pairwise angles as edges, to reconstruct each detector's calibration offset.

Applied to eight Planck NPIPE detector-set maps, the network reconstruction agrees with the MK calibration pattern (χ² = 8.18 for 7 degrees of freedom, PTE = 0.32), with no map deviating by more than 1.8σ. I will explain what this does and does not tell us. Because both methods use the same maps, this is an independent method rather than independent data. It supports the calibration foundation of the β hint but cannot fix its absolute zero point.

I will close by discussing how a sub-0.1° external calibration anchor, combined with this network, could deliver an absolute birefringence measurement. This will be possible with BICEP/Keck, SPT-3G, the Simons Observatory, and LiteBIRD.

About the Astro/Cosmology Seminar series:
The Center for Dark Cosmology and Gravitation seminar series (aka, the Department of Physics Astrophysics and Cosmology Seminar) will showcase key developments in astrophysics and cosmology, the implications of these for fundamental physics, and vice versa, the implications of laboratory particle physics discoveries for our understanding of the cosmos. Among the outstanding issues in physics, the nature of the dark matter and dark energy and the origin of the supermassive black holes very early in the history of the universe stand out as venues where beyond standard model physics is at play or likely plays a role. The pace of discovery in this field is breathtaking. The advent of gravitational wave observatories, the James Webb Space Telescope, and the Simons Observatory for the cosmic microwave background all complement a host of laboratory experiments including LHC, short and long baseline neutrino oscillation experiments, neutrino less double beta decay searches, and direct dark matter detection experiments, to name just a few. Moreover, all of these research thrusts are underpinned by rapid development of computational capabilities and artificial intelligence. The CDCG is dedicated to facilitating and bridging laboratory, observational, theoretical and computational studies focussed on the cosmos.

title: Tuning Quantum Materials with Extreme Pressure and Magnetic Field
speaker: Yuhang Deng (Dept. of Physics, UCSD)
abstract:
Abstract: Correlated electron materials based on lanthanides, actinides, and transition metals host a rich landscape of emergent phenomena, including unconventional superconductivity, exotic magnetism, heavy-fermion behavior, and nontrivial topological states. These phenomena emerge from the interplay among strong electronic correlations, spin–orbit coupling, and competing energy scales, and can be dramatically modified by external parameters such as pressure, magnetic field, and chemical composition.

In this talk, I will discuss our efforts to uncover and control quantum phases in correlated materials under extreme conditions of high pressure and high magnetic fields. Using diamond anvil cells, which enable electrical, magnetic, and optical measurements at high pressures, together with complementary high-field techniques, we investigate how these tuning parameters
reshape electronic, magnetic, and structural properties. I will highlight three examples: pressure-induced metallization and suppression of a magnetically ordered conducting surface state in FeSi; pressure-driven structural and valence evolution, and new superconductivity in UTe 2 ; and the emergence and evolution of multiple superconducting states in U 1-x Th x Te 2 under high magnetic fields. Together, these studies demonstrate how pressure, magnetic field, and chemical substitution can tune the delicate balance among competing interactions in correlated electron systems, providing new perspectives on the mechanisms underlying unconventional superconductivity, magnetism, and topological quantum states.

Yuhang Deng received his Ph.D. in Physics from Washington University in St. Louis in 2019. He subsequently joined Prof. M. Brian Maple’s group at the University of California San Diego, where he worked as a postdoctoral scholar and is currently an Assistant Project Scientist. His research focuses on the experimental study of quantum materials under extreme conditions, particularly superconductivity and magnetism at high pressures and high magnetic fields. His broader research interests include topological and Kondo insulators, unconventional superconductors, and the application of diamond nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers to high-pressure physics.

title: Modeling density variations in microtubule-based two-dimensional active nematics
speaker: Kevin  Mitchell (UC Merced)
abstract: Abstract: A dense two-dimensional layer of aligned microtubules (MTs), powered by molecular motors, is a canonical laboratory model of active materials and a synthetic analog of biological systems such as bacterial turbulence, mitotic spindles, and morphogenesis. This material exhibits nematic ordering and associated topological defects, which display complex emergent dynamics, including the creation and annihilation of defects and the braiding of defects around one another in a complicated chaotic dance. Despite its prominent role in research, the MT-based active nematic material lacks a well established theoretical model that accurately captures the rich density variations prominently seen in experiments—--density variations that are, in fact, the experimental signature of the nematic structure itself. The MT-system is typically modeled using two fields: the Q-tensor (encoding the order and orientation of the nematic phase) and the fluid velocity; critically, the microtubule density is assumed to be constant. This traditional model is adopted from classical Landau-de Gennes liquid crystal theory. In this talk, we present a fundamentally different approach to modeling MT-based active nematics that explicitly incorporates density variations, producing simulations that strongly resemble experimental videos, including the characteristic striation patterns. It also reproduces important behavior of the system confined to a circular well—behavior seen experimentally, but not captured by current theory. In crafting our model, we present an alternative to Landau-de Gennes theory for the creation and annihilation of topological defects that does not rely on the classic isotropic-nematic phase transition.

title: From Preons to Flavor: Testing Quark and Lepton Compositeness
speaker: Amartya Sengupta (University of Buffalo)
abstract:
Abstract:
A composite origin of quarks and leptons could connect the observed fermion masses and mixing angles to new strong dynamics. In this talk, we study a renormalizable preon model based on a confining chiral SU(15) gauge theory, in which Standard Model fermions—and possibly the Higgs—emerge as bound states of more fundamental constituents. We show that a simple hierarchy in two flavor-breaking couplings can reproduce all six quark masses, the charged-lepton masses, and the CKM matrix, with nonperturbative parameters of order unity. The same couplings induce flavor- and CP-violating effects, allowing low-energy measurements to probe the model even when the compositeness scale lies beyond collider reach. We discuss the constraints from the electron electric dipole moment, neutral-meson mixing, and charged-lepton flavor violation, and compare their sensitivity with that of proton-decay searches.

title: Planckian Dynamics in Quantum Matter
speaker: Debanjan Chowdhury (Cornell University)
abstract:
Abstract:
A long-standing puzzle in strongly correlated quantum matter is the ubiquity of a Planckian timescale governing transport, appearing across disparate materials and largely independent of microscopic details. Despite extensive experimental evidence, this phenomenon has proven notoriously difficult to capture within conventional theoretical frameworks. In this colloquium, I will first explain why achieving microscopic control over Planckian dynamics is so challenging. I will then discuss a concrete example of a correlated material in which Planckian behavior can be understood from first principles. Finally, I will survey recent progress toward deriving rigorous Planckian bounds, drawing on ideas from quantum information, many-body physics, and nonequilibrium statistical mechanics. Together, these developments suggest that Planckian dynamics may arise from fundamental constraints on thermalization and information flow in quantum matter.

title: The Dark Dimension, Revisited
speaker: Vincent Lee (UC Berkeley / N3AS)
abstract: Abstract: Motivated by the swampland program, it has been proposed that a tower of massive Kaluza-Klein (KK) gravitons from a compactified flat extra dimension can be dark matter, with the heavier modes constantly cascading to lighter ones. The phenomenology crucially depends on the rate at which a massive KK mode decays to lighter modes. We show that, up to mild assumptions on the UV theory, the decay rate is suppressed by a factor of (q/m)^4 compared to the one commonly used in the literature, where q is the momentum of the decay products and m is the mass of the decaying KK mode. This suggests that the proposed scenario is ruled out by CMB observations by many orders of magnitude. Remarkably, the same suppression opens up a vastly different parameter space in which KK gravitons from a strongly warped extra dimension (e.g. a Randall-Sundrum setup) are a viable dark matter candidate, either as the cascading gravitons themselves or as a stable component of the tower. We discuss the corresponding phenomenology, and prospects in detecting such dark matter with astrophysical observations.

title: RG improved (optimized) perturbation: chiral symmetry breaking and QCD thermodynamics
speaker: Jean-Loic Kneur (University of Montpellier)
abstract:
Abstract: We discuss a specific Renormalization Group (RG) resummation of perturbative expansions that can give nontrivial results for the order parameters of chiral symmetry breaking in QCD. We illustrate in particular the quark condensate obtained up to five-loop order using the Dirac spectral density and related Banks-Casher relation, and compared to Lattice QCD results. We then discuss extensions of this approach to hot QCD, or to cold and dense QCD. For hot QCD a drastically reduced residual renormalization scale dependence is obtained as compared to standard perturbative QCD. For cold and dense quark matter the three-loop RG-improved equation of state is used to obtain mass-radius relations for pure quark or hybrid hadron-quark compact stars, which are compared to recent astrophysical observations.

Speaker Biography: Jean-Loic Kneur is currently the CNRS Director of Research in the Charles Coulomb Lab in Montpellier, France. His main research topics have included: higher order corrections in Standard Model and supersymmetric models, supersymmetry and neutralino dark matter phenomenology, composite (pseudo-Goldstone) Higgs models, Effective Theories for thermal QCD (Hard Thermal Loop), and more recently, applications to neutron stars.

title: A Witten effect for global monopoles
speaker: Pablo Quílez Lasanta
abstract:
Abstract:

Global monopoles can carry electric charge even when the scalar fields that form them are neutral. I will show how an interaction usually discarded as a total derivative produces a Witten effect for these global defects, giving them an electric charge proportional to their winding number. I will explain its origin and illustrate the mechanism in a simple UV completion.

Based on arXiv:2610.14168 [hep-ph]

Bio:
Pablo Quílez Lasanta received his PhD from the Universidad Autónoma de Madrid and the Instituto de Física Teórica (IFT), followed by postdoctoral positions at DESY (Hamburg) and UC San Diego. He is currently a Marie Skłodowska-Curie Fellow at CERN, and will join the University of Barcelona next year on a tenure-track position. His research focuses on axions and axion-like particles, effective field theories and Hilbert series, and more recently on formal aspects of partial-wave unitarity and topological defects.

title: Superconductivity and magnetism in crystalline graphite allotropes
speaker: Andrea Young (UC Santa Barbara)
abstract: I will describe the physics of graphite crystals with rhombohedral stacking, where the competition between electron hopping within- and between- the graphene planes leads to a flat electronic dispersion and the crystallinity leads to a near total absence of disorder. The high electronic density of states and Berry curvature—-both of which can be tuned by a perpendicular electric field—lead to a dizzying variety of magnetic and superconducting states, often within the same device, while the high experimental reproducibility enabled by the crystalline nature of these structurally simple systems allows us to investigate a variety of correlated electron phenomena. I will focus on our efforts to use scanning nanoscale magnetometry to probe the nature and origins of magnetism and unconventional superconductivity, as well as the fate of the correlated electron liquid at high temperatures.

title: Fluids within Solids
speaker: Fazel Tafti (Boston College)
abstract:
Abstract: I will present recent results from my group that demonstrate fluid-like states in solid materials. I start by presenting new advances in finding metallic specimens with extremely large conductivity, and show how such materials might enter the hydrostatic limit of electronic transport. I will particularly show our most recent results on NbGe2 , NbSi2 , TaGe2 , and TaSi2 that showcase a beautiful example of tuning electron-phonon coupling and reveal its influence on quantum and transport mobility. Next, I will present our recent results in engineering a new generation of Kitaev materials, where bond directional interactions lead to the emergence of a quantum spin liquid with fractionalized anionic particles. I will show how physical and chemical pressure have been used to tune the magnetic interactions in these systems.

Speaker Biography: Fazel Tafti completed his PhD at the University of Toronto with Prof. Stephen Julian. His thesis was focused on developing transport experiments under ultrahigh pressures in diamond anvil cells. His first postdoc position at the University of Sherbrooke with Prof. Louis Taillefer was focused on the thermal conductivity and thermoelectric measurements in iron-based superconductors under intense magnetic fields. He then changed fields from physics to chemistry and completed a second postdoc at Princeton University with Prof. Bob Cava. His research was focused on the chemical synthesis of topological and magnetic materials. He started his career at Boston College in 2016 where he is currently a tenured associate professor of physics. His lab at BC is interdisciplinary between physics, chemistry, and materials science.

title: What is the dynamical exponent of two-dimensional Fermi liquids?
speaker: Thomas Scaffidi (UC Irvine)
abstract: Over the past decade, experiments in clean materials have revealed that electrons in a solid can flow like a viscous fluid governed by the Navier–Stokes equations. This raises a fundamental question: can the fermionic nature of electrons give rise to a different kind of hydrodynamics? The answer turns out to be yes in two dimensions: long-lived parity-odd deformations of a circular Fermi surface act as additional quasi-conserved quantities, giving rise to a distinct, so-called tomographic regime. In this talk, I will show how this departure from conventional hydrodynamics extends to the dynamical realm. Starting from a microscopic numerical evaluation of the linearized electron–electron collision operator, we find that the nonlocal conductivity in the tomographic regime is controlled at low frequency by a single hydrodynamic pole, (\sigma(q,\omega)=D(q)/(i\omega+\eta_\star q^z)), with dynamical exponent (z=4/3) and superdiffusive viscosity (\eta_\star). Remarkably, the Drude weight is itself scale dependent, obeying (D(q)\sim q^{-\alpha}) with (\alpha=1/3), so the dynamical response is characterized by two distinct exponents rather than one. Finally, I will discuss how AC transport in narrow channels provides a direct experimental probe of these two scaling laws.
